title: Ready to leave
hook: act, speak and think as one who could leave life at any moment (Meditations 2.11)

segments.voice: Yesterday: attend to your own soul, the flashlight turned inward. Your line was mind my own mind. What did you find moving in there? Day five hundred thirty-five.

People who travel a lot often keep a bag half packed. Toothbrush, charger, a clean shirt. When the call comes, they can be out the door in ten minutes, without panic. Nothing important is left undone, because they keep it that way. In book two, in a camp where death was never far off, Marcus writes himself a note about living like that. Not about wanting to go. About being the kind of person who could, without leaving a mess of unsaid things behind. Today: ready to leave.
screen: `A BAG HALF PACKED.` → `NOTHING IMPORTANT LEFT UNDONE.` → `READY TO LEAVE.`

segments.voice: First, the instruction. Section eleven begins: since you could leave life at any moment, let that shape every action, every word and every thought. It's not a threat. It's an editing rule. If this might be the last thing I do, is this how I want to do it? Second, the reasoning. Marcus then thinks out loud about what leaving means. If there are gods, he says, departing isn't something to fear, because they wouldn't bring you into harm. If there were no gods, or they didn't care, why would he want to live in a world empty of them? Then he says plainly what he believes: they do exist, and they do care. People today read that passage from many places: some share his faith, some don't, some aren't sure. What all of them can notice is that he reasoned his way to calm, not away from the question. Third, what isn't the point. Life and death, praise and blame, pain and pleasure, money and its lack, he says, happen to good and bad people alike. So they can't be what makes a life good or bad. What makes it good is how you live it. Fourth, ready. Ready doesn't mean waiting to go, or wanting to. It means not leaving the important things for later. The apology. The thank you. The I love you you assume they know. A traveler with a half-packed bag isn't hoping to leave. They're just free to live without dread. That's what Marcus wanted: not a shorter life, a fuller one, lived so that any moment could be the last one and still be all right.
screen: `YOU COULD LEAVE AT ANY MOMENT.` · `HE REASONED HIS WAY TO CALM.` · `THESE COME TO GOOD AND BAD ALIKE.` · `READY: NOTHING IMPORTANT LEFT FOR LATER.` · then, large: `READY.`

segments.voice: This can feel heavy, so go gently. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you'd regret leaving unsaid or undone if today were your last ordinary day. A thank you. An apology. A call to someone you love. Just one. Picture doing it today, simply, without drama. Notice how much lighter the rest of the day feels with it done. The bell holds the time.
Ready to leave. Marcus: since you could leave life at any moment, let that shape every act, word and thought, and leave nothing important for later. Today's word.
Your line: ready. Do one thing today you'd hate to leave undone: say the thank you, make the call, mend the small break. Day five hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Many people who practice Stoicism use the thought of death as a prompt not to postpone what matters, such as apologies, thanks and time with people they love.

fork.setup: you owe someone an apology. it's awkward, and there's always next week. what does Meditations 2.11 suggest?
options: do it today, as one who could leave at any time.
let it go; they've probably forgotten.
fork.reveal: since you could leave life at any moment, Marcus says, let that shape every act, word and thought.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gloomy reminder that you'll die.
what it means: an editing rule for each act, so nothing important is left for later, and the day is lived without dread.
what a scholar hears: 2.11 reasons through 'gods or no gods' before affirming providence, an argument Marcus returns to elsewhere in the notebook.

notes: Meditations 2.11 paraphrased: since it is possible to depart life this moment, regulate every act and thought accordingly; if gods exist, departing is not to be feared; if not, or if they don't care, why live in a universe void of gods and providence; but they exist and care; life and death, honor and dishonor, pain and pleasure, riches and poverty happen equally to good and bad, so are neither good nor evil. Confirm.
